FRB: FEDS Notes en FEDS Note: Europe’s Natural Gas Outlook for the Upcoming Winter 2026/2027 Johannes Fleck

Europe is entering the 2026–27 winter with unusually low natural gas inventories. At the end of September 2026, gas storage in the EU was about 72 percent full, the lowest fill rate for that month since EU-wide data are available (from 2011) and about 11 percentage points below last September.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: When productivity booms, do interest rates rise? Antoine Lepetit, and David Miller

Long-term interest rates have risen sharply since the COVID period. Concurrently, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have raised the prospect of a sustained increase in productivity growth. As many observers have noted, standard macroeconomic theory predicts that expectations of faster productivity growth should push interest rates higher.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Increasing International Interdependence: Global Supply Chains and Cross-Border Macroeconomic Spillovers Francois de Soyres

International production is increasingly organized through networks of firms that source inputs, assemble products, and supply customers across borders. As these networks deepen, conditions in one country matter more for output and prices in another, so domestic outcomes depend less on domestic conditions alone and more on the economies and sectors on which domestic production relies.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets Christine Dobridge, Tim Dore, Simon Glossner, Elizabeth Holmquist, Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek, and Irina Stefanescu

The expansion of private credit has become one of the most significant developments in financial markets over the past decade. Yet, estimates of the size of the market vary considerably, in part because the term private credit is used to describe different instruments, investment strategies, and financial intermediaries.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: A Common Pattern behind Diverging Fortunes: U.S. Tariffs and Exports from Canada and Mexico Musa Orak, and Avani Pradhan

The 2025 U.S. tariff increases were followed by sharply different export outcomes in Canada and Mexico. Comparing the 12 months ending in April 2026 with calendar year 2024, Canadian goods exports to the United States fell about 10 percent, while Mexican exports rose about 16 percent, even though Mexico faced a higher average tariff exposure (figure 1). Do these contrasting outcomes mean that tariffs mattered for Canada but had little effect on Mexico, even though both economies depend heavily on the U.S. market?]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Gold Reserve Relocations: Are They Always Bad News for U.S. Dollar Reserves? Colin Weiss

This note reviews several publicized gold reserve relocations by central banks in the Netherlands, France, and Germany since 2013 and any concurrent changes in their U.S. dollar reserve allocations. Generally, the choice of where to custody gold reserves may in part reflect the perceived risk of sanctions or expropriation in the jurisdiction of custody alongside other considerations like the proximity to international gold markets.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies Andrea De Michelis, Musa Orak, Avani Pradhan, and Albert Queralto

Elevated oil prices and heightened geopolitical uncertainty have renewed interest in a longstanding policy question: do supply shocks like oil-price increases pose a transitory or a persistent threat to price stability? This note sheds light on this question by providing new evidence on whether the inflation process has changed.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Treasury Issuance and Dealer Balance Sheets Lubomir Petrasek, Zack Saravay, and Mary Tian

Primary dealers play an important role as intermediaries in Treasury securities and repo markets, and demand for their intermediation rises on issuance dates. Recent increases in Treasury issuance have raised questions about dealers' capacity to meet this increased demand.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Government Bonds’ Safe-Haven Property and Inflationary Pressures Canlin Li and Emre Yoldas

Earlier this year, escalation of the conflict in the Middle East resulted in sharp declines in major stock indexes as energy prices rose and the global economic outlook deteriorated, but prices of long-term government bonds in major advanced economies also declined (Figure 1). This prompted some commentators to question the premise that government bonds in these major advanced economies will rally in times of increased risk aversion and serve as a safe haven for investors (see for example, Kim, 2026).]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Ripples in the Reserve Pool: Unveiling Liquidity Signals from the Federal Funds Market Sriya Anbil, Sebastian Infante, and Zeynep Senyuz

When the Federal Reserve shifted to an ample-reserves framework, many observers started to question the relevance of the fed funds market. With reserves ample or abundant and rates anchored by administered floors, interbank borrowing declined sharply, and the market appeared to serve mainly as an arbitrage venue for non-bank institutions.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States Christine Dobridge, Tim Dore, Simon Glossner, Elizabeth Holmquist, Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek, and Irina Stefanescu

Over the past decade, private credit has played an increasingly important role in providing funding to middle-market businesses. While there are several definitions of private credit, here we define it as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds rather than by traditional financial intermediaries such as banks.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: The Rise of Semiliquid Funds for Retail Investors Chaehee Shin

Investment funds differ in how investors can access their capital. The redemption rules governing how and when investors can withdraw have evolved endogenously in response to shifting investor demand and regulatory constraints. While the immediate liquidity of open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds has long dominated the retail market, the landscape has been evolving over time.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Convenience Yields, Risk Premiums, and the Interpretation of Oil Futures Prices During Times of Geopolitical Conflict Erik Heitfield, Yang-Ho Park and Erfan Danesh

Earlier this year the Middle East conflict led to one of the largest global oil supply shocks in history (Bordoff and O'Sullivan, 2026). Past empirical research has found that commodity futures prices provide accurate predictions of future spot prices under normal market conditions (Reeve and Vigfusson, 2011; Chernenko et al., 2004).]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Beyond the Current Account: U.S. Financial Flows and Global Imbalances Cody Kallen and Alexandra Tabova

Global imbalances have returned to the center of international policy discussions, including at the G7 and G20. These discussions have traditionally focused on current account (CA) balances and, in particular, on the drivers and consequences of persistent trade surpluses and deficits.]]> FEDS Notes FEDS Note: Assessing Monetary Policy Globally: Evidence from LLMs and Semi-structural Models Diego Vilán

Over the past decades, central bank communication has become an increasingly important component of modern monetary policy frameworks. Policy rates, asset purchases, and balance-sheet tools remain central to the transmission of monetary policy, but speeches, press conferences, forward guidance, and other forms of public communication have all played a direct role in shaping expectations about the future path of policy.]]> FEDS Notes
